title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
summary:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

title: Building a browser GIF editor: the frame memory limit matters more than file size
summary:
I built VisualFormat, a free set of browser GIF tools. The files are processed locally, with no account required. One practical constraint shaped the implementation: a small GIF file can still be expensive to decode.

Start with decoded pixels

A 1,000 × 1,000 animation with 100 frames represents 100 million frame pixels. At four bytes per RGBA pixel, keeping a full decoded copy of every frame would already take roughly 400 MB, before working canvases and encoding buffers. The compressed download size does not describe that cost.

VisualFormat scans GIF blocks before allocating decoded frames. It checks dimensions, frame count and the total canvas pixels across the animation. The current GIF input limits are 20 MB, 500 frames, 4,096 pixels per dimension and 40 million total frame pixels. These are guardrails, not a guarantee that every device can process every accepted file.

title: AI vs Human WordPress Writing
summary:
A comparison of AI writing tools and human writers for WordPress content.

Should we embrace AI for content creation or stick with human writers? After extensive testing with both approaches, below is what I found.

The Reality of AI Writing Tools

AI writing has evolved beyond the keyword-stuffing bots of yesterday. Modern tools like Claude and GPT-4 produce grammatically correct, coherent content that reads naturally. They excel at technical documentation, code generation, and scaling content production. What takes human writers hours happens in minutes.

Yet AI tools struggle with nuanced understanding from real-world experience. When we write about debugging WordPress plugin conflicts at 2 AM or handling client scope creep, that authenticity resonates. AI describes these scenarios without living them. The consistency of AI output becomes both strength and weakness, plateauing at “good enough” for most use cases.

title: From Onboarding to Production: How I Built Dynamic Vendor Switching at Wise
summary:
When I joined Wise, I was expecting the standard new-joiner experience: documentation, shadowing sessions, maybe a small bug fix or two to ease in. What I got instead was a real problem, a blank design doc, and a team ready to help me solve it.

That problem became my onboarding project, a system that automatically switches payment vendors when one of them starts failing, and that now quietly handles real customer payments every day.

title: CodeSOD: Death of the Auth-Er

When writing Perl, it's not unusual to want to die. The die function ends your Perl program with an error string, and you'll often see code like: die "My error" unless $i > 5 or die "Other error" if check(), because Perl just loves the backwards conditionals. What's even more fun with die is how it behaves with eval blocks, so it doesn't always kill your program, sometimes it is how you pass error strings back out of sections of your program.
